clue.text: Surpass everyone — but you may stop playing!

definitions.text: Surpass everyone
definitions.meaning: to beat the best performance anyone has ever achieved

definitions.text: you may stop playing
definitions.meaning: smashing a gramophone disc would certainly end the music

explanation.surface: A champion outdoes all rivals, yet the triumph might bring the game to a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting a new best mark is the idiom; literally cracking a vinyl disc stops it playing.

clue.text: Not a place for one of the great bats.

definitions.text: Not a place for one of the great bats.

parts.words: Not a place for one of the great bats.
parts.note: in a cricket batting order the last slot of the side goes to the weakest batsman, never a star

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' means batsmen, not flying mammals; a cricket team has eleven players, and the last in the order is usually a bowler who can barely bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket convention: the final position in the batting order is kept for the poorest batsman.

clue.text: "Andmountainous heaped For truth to o'erpeer

definitions.text: "Andmountainous heaped For truth to o'erpeer

parts.note: a line from Coriolanus with one word left out: 'And mountainous ___ be too highly heap'd For truth to o'erpeer'

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Shakespeare's Coriolanus; the missing word is the answer. The OCR has run 'And' and 'mountainous' together.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted line speaks of mistakes piled so high that truth could not see over them.

clue.text: There's nothing going to waste here-it's merely supposing.

definitions.text: merely supposing

parts.note: nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O
pining means wasting away

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that nothing is being squandered here; it is only a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a view without proof is simply to suppose or hold an opinion.

clue.text: Selfish brute, won't let others hit the hay?

definitions.text: Selfish brute, won't let others hit the hay?

parts.words: Selfish brute, won't let others hit the hay?
parts.note: the fable of a hound lying in a feeding trough of hay that it cannot eat, keeping the ox from it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit the hay' usually means go to bed; here it is literal, the cattle being kept from their fodder by Aesop's dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a spiteful person who stops others enjoying what they cannot use themselves.

clue.text: The, outcome no doubt of too many sweeps.

definitions.text: The, outcome no doubt of too many sweeps.

parts.words: The, outcome no doubt of too many sweeps.
parts.note: a servant who spends hours kneeling to sweep and scrub floors develops a swollen joint

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweeps' suggests chimney sweeps or betting; it means sweeping floors on one's knees. The stray comma after 'The' is an OCR blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Prepatellar bursitis was named after domestic servants whose kneeling work inflamed the kneecap.

clue.text: Quantities produced

definitions.text: Quantities produced

parts.note: a plain description of the amounts a factory or worker turns out

explanation.definitionFit: Production figures for a plant or machine are its yields.

clue.text: Grainer, could be wrongly used for ac.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Grainer, could be wrongly used for ac.', is cut short: the anagram of GRAINER is there but the definition ('ac...') is missing
annotationWithheld.clue: Grainer, could be wrongly used for ac.

clue.text: Not a complimentary remark.

definitions.text: Not a complimentary remark.

parts.note: a comment that finds fault rather than praising

explanation.definitionFit: A censure or adverse criticism is the opposite of a compliment.

clue.text: It's the span of a ruler.

definitions.text: It's the span of a ruler.

parts.words: It's the span of a ruler.
parts.note: a measuring stick's length, read instead as the period a monarch is on the throne

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' suggests a twelve-inch measuring stick; it is a sovereign, and the span is time, not length.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign's time in power is measured from accession to death or abdication.

clue.text: Very smart are they — or just posers?

definitions.text: Very smart are they — or just posers?

parts.words: Very smart are they — or just posers?
parts.note: fashionable people who sit or stand for artists and photographers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Posers' sounds like an insult for show-offs, but these people literally pose for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Mannequins and artists' sitters are elegantly dressed people paid to hold poses.

clue.text: One way to lie.

definitions.text: One way to lie.

parts.note: stretched out fully, rather than telling an untruth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' tempts towards fibbing; it means reclining, and the phrase also means in detail or finally.
explanation.definitionFit: To recline full-stretch is to lie with the body extended.

clue.text: One sort of idea — a cert to pull out.

definitions.text: pull out

indicators.note: the letters given take one particular rearranged form, a different sort of arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone with a notion considers a sure thing worth withdrawing from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One sort of' signals that IDEA, A and CERT are rearranged together; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To uproot or extract something completely is to remove it root and all.

clue.text: Just what's wanted for a post-nuptial fling.

definitions.text: Just what's wanted for a post-nuptial fling.

parts.words: Just what's wanted for a post-nuptial fling.
parts.note: a fling is a throw: guests toss paper pieces over a newly married couple

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' suggests an affair after marriage; it means a throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Small paper scraps are thrown over bride and groom as they leave the church.

clue.text: Picture perhaps of a domestic scene.

definitions.text: Picture perhaps of a domestic scene.

parts.words: Picture perhaps of a domestic scene.
parts.note: a painting showing the inside of a home, as Dutch masters often did

explanation.definitionFit: An art-history term for a painting depicting a room inside a house.

clue.text: Where one can always study the fare.

definitions.text: Where one can always study the fare.

parts.words: Where one can always study the fare.
parts.note: the menu sense of fare is a decoy: a meter shows the price of the ride

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' suggests food on a menu; it is the passenger's charge, displayed on the meter.
explanation.definitionFit: In a hired cab the meter in front of the passenger shows the running charge.

clue.text: A measure of understanding.

definitions.text: A measure of understanding.

parts.note: a unit of depth, six feet, that also as a verb means to grasp

explanation.definitionFit: It is both a nautical depth unit and a verb for comprehending.

clue.text: Its occupant isn't usually anxious for self-display

definitions.text: Its occupant isn't usually anxious for self-display

parts.words: Its occupant isn't usually anxious for self-display
parts.note: a fugitive's lair, whose resident is keen not to be seen

explanation.definitionFit: A secret refuge is used by someone wishing to stay concealed.

clue.text: "A a villain, lost to love and truth" (Burns).

definitions.text: "A a villain, lost to love and truth" (Burns).

parts.words: "A a villain, lost to love and truth" (Burns).
parts.note: a line from The Cotter's Saturday Night with one word left out: 'A ___! a villain! lost to love and truth!'

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Robert Burns; the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns describes a seducer as a miserable, despicable creature.

clue.text: Definitely a big hit.

definitions.text: Definitely a big hit.

parts.note: in cricket, a stroke clearing the boundary without bouncing scores the maximum six runs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big hit' suggests a smash success; it is a cricket stroke worth six runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket slang for a shot over the boundary rope scoring six.

clue.text: Like one of those Rides of Cobbett.

definitions.text: Like one of those Rides of Cobbett.

parts.words: Like one of those Rides of Cobbett.
parts.note: William Cobbett's 1830 book recounts his horseback tours of the English countryside

explanation.walkthrough: Cobbett's famous book is titled after these countryside journeys, so each ride is of the countryside kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobbett's book title describes journeys through farmland and villages.

clue.text: Like the earliest of apples.

definitions.text: Like the earliest of apples.

parts.note: the first apple in Genesis, which Adam and Eve were told not to eat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Earliest' suggests a fruit variety; it is the fruit in the Garden of Eden.
explanation.definitionFit: Eden's fruit was banned by God, giving the phrase for a tempting prohibited thing.
